## What is a Collection Letter?


A collection letter is a formal written notice sent to a customer who hasn’t paid an overdue invoice, asking them to settle the balance by a set date. It’s usually sent after friendly reminders have gone unanswered, and it escalates in tone over time, from a formal reminder to a final notice before legal action.


Collection letters are sometimes called collection notices. Whatever you call them, they cover an[outstanding invoice](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/outstanding-invoices) and mark a more serious stage in the[accounts receivable process](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/accounts-receivable-process) , typically once[email reminders](https://upflow.io/blog/payment-reminders/payment-reminders) or[phone calls](https://upflow.io/blog/payment-reminders/collection-calls) haven’t led to payment.


A well-structured collection letter includes the amount due, the invoice numbers, the payment terms, a deadline for payment and clear instructions on how to pay. Later letters in the sequence also explain the consequences of not paying, such as late fees, restricted access to your services or legal action.


Before moving to collection letters, it’s best to start with polite[collection emails](https://upflow.io/blog/payment-reminders/collection-emails) . Click the banner below to download our free collection email templates.


## Collection Letter Templates and Samples


Below are four collection letter samples you can copy and adapt, in the order you’d usually send them. They escalate from a formal reminder of the amount due to a legal notice, so each letter raises the urgency only when the previous one hasn’t worked.


### Collection Letter Sample 1: Formal Reminder of Due Payment


Send this first letter when earlier emails, phone calls or even[SMS](https://upflow.io/blog/payment-reminders/payment-reminder-message) reminders haven’t led to payment. It summarizes the outstanding invoices, explains how to pay, and asks the client to act now to avoid further escalation.


Here’s a copy-paste version:


Subject: Reminder: Payment Due for Invoice No. \[Invoice number\]


Dear \[Client Name\],


I hope this message finds you well. We are writing to follow up on several outstanding invoices that have yet to be settled, despite previous email reminders and phone calls regarding the overdue payment.


Currently, the total amount due is \[Total amount\], with the oldest invoice overdue by \[Number\] days. Please find a summary of the overdue invoices below:


- Invoice Number: \[Invoice number\]
- Amount: \[Invoice amount\]
- Due Date: \[Due date\]


You will find a copy of the original invoice(s) attached for your reference. We kindly request that payment be made immediately upon receipt of this letter.


Payment methods:
You can make a payment using the following methods:
\[Payment instructions\]


If payment is not received by \[Specific date\], we will be forced to take further action, which may include restricting access to our services.


Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.


Best regards,
\[Your Name\]
\[Your Contact Info\]
\[Your Company Name\]


### Collection Letter Sample 2: Warning of Service Restriction


This second letter warns the client that access to your services or products will be restricted if the balance isn’t paid within a set number of days. The tone is firmer, and it makes clear that the delay now has consequences.


Copy and adapt this version:


Subject: Clear Invoice No. \[Invoice number\] to Avoid Service Disruption


Dear \[Client Name\],


We are reaching out once again regarding your outstanding invoices, which now total \[Total amount\]. Despite our previous communications, payment has not been received for the overdue invoices listed below:


- Invoice Number: \[Invoice number\]
- Amount: \[Invoice amount\]
- Due Date: \[Due date\]


We have attached copies of the outstanding invoices for your reference. Please note that as per our terms and conditions, if payment is not received within \[Number\] days, we will regrettably be forced to restrict access to your account/services until the balance is settled.


To avoid any service disruptions, we request immediate payment via the following methods:
\[Payment instructions\]


We appreciate your urgent attention to this matter and hope to resolve it promptly to avoid further escalation.


Best regards,
\[Your Name\]
\[Your Contact Info\]
\[Your Company Name\]


### Collection Letter Sample 3: Final Notice Before Legal Action


Use this letter once services have been restricted. It confirms the restriction, sets a final deadline, and warns that legal action will follow if the balance stays unpaid. It also leaves room to agree on a payment plan, which is often the quickest way to recover the money at this stage.


Use this text as your starting point:


Subject: Service Restricted Due to Non-Payment: Final Notice Before Legal Action


Dear \[Client Name\],


Despite multiple reminders and previous communication, we have yet to receive payment for the overdue invoices listed below, which now total \[Total amount\]. As a result, we have restricted your access to our services, effective immediately.


Outstanding invoices:


- Invoice Number: \[Invoice number\]
- Amount: \[Invoice amount\]
- Due Date: \[Due date\]


Copies of all overdue invoices are attached for your reference. We demand that you settle the outstanding amount within \[Number\] days. If payment is not received by this date, we will have no choice but to initiate legal action and seek compensation for the financial loss incurred due to non-payment.


We are still open to discussing a payment plan if required. Please reach out immediately if this is of interest to you.


You can make the payment using the following methods:
\[Payment instructions\]


Best regards,
\[Your Name\]
\[Your Contact Info\]
\[Your Company Name\]


### Collection Letter Sample 4: Legal Notice


This last letter is for when legal proceedings have already started. It informs the client of the action taken, explains that penalties, legal fees or interest may be added, and still gives them a way to settle. Requirements for legal notices vary by country and state, so check with your legal counsel before sending it.


Copy the full letter below:


Subject: Legal Action Initiated for Non-Payment


Dear \[Client Name\],


We regret to inform you that due to your continued failure to settle the outstanding balance of \[Total amount\], we have initiated legal proceedings to recover the debt.


Despite our multiple reminders and service restrictions, the following invoices remain unpaid:


- Invoice Number: \[Invoice number\]
- Amount: \[Invoice amount\]
- Due Date: \[Due date\]


Copies of the invoices are attached for your reference. Legal action has already been taken, and we urge you to make immediate payment to avoid further penalties, legal fees, or interest that may accumulate as the process moves forward.


You can still resolve this matter by making payment via the following methods:
\[Payment instructions\]


Please contact us immediately if you wish to discuss settling this debt to avoid further escalation.


Sincerely,
\[Your Name\]
\[Your Contact Info\]
\[Your Company Name\]


## What to Include in a Collection Letter (Format Checklist)


A collection letter should make it easy for the customer to see what they owe, why and how to pay. Most effective letters follow the same format: a clear subject line, a short opening that states the overdue balance, a list of the unpaid invoices, payment instructions, a deadline, and the next steps if the deadline passes.


Here’s what to include:


1. **Personal details.** Address the letter to the right person by name, with their company name and a reference to the products or services you’ve provided.
2. **Your contact information.** Give your business address, email and phone number, so the customer can easily reach you with questions.
3. **Copies of all overdue invoices.** Attach every overdue invoice, and list them in the body of the letter if there’s more than one, so the customer sees each balance clearly.
4. **Invoice details and due dates.** Reference the invoice numbers, the amounts owed and how many days each is overdue.
5. **Late fees, if applicable.** If your terms allow[late fees](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/late-fee) , include an updated invoice showing them, and explain whether they’ll keep adding up.
6. **Payment methods.** List the[payment methods](https://upflow.io/blog/business-to-business-payments/b2b-payment-methods) you accept, such as card, bank transfer or a payment link. A direct link is often the fastest way to get paid.
7. **A payment plan (optional).** If the customer is struggling, offer to spread the balance over weekly or monthly payments.
8. **Consequences of non-payment.** Explain what happens next if the deadline passes, such as suspending services, passing the debt to a[receivable management services](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/receivable-management-services-alternatives) company or taking legal action, and reference the contract terms that allow it.


Keep the tone clear and professional throughout. A letter that’s easy to act on gets paid faster and protects the relationship better than one that’s simply forceful.


## When to Send a Collection Letter: The Escalation Timeline


Send your first collection letter once an invoice is around 30 days overdue and earlier reminder emails and phone calls haven’t worked. Then escalate roughly every two weeks, from a formal reminder to a final notice and, as a last resort, a legal notice.


A good collection strategy balances persistence with respect for the relationship. Emilie Hart, who leads the Finance Operations team at[WorkMotion](https://upflow.io/customers/workmotion) , puts it this way:


"Our main goal is to create a positive customer experience when it comes to collections by ensuring we're sending and triggering reminders when it matters most."


Emilie Hart


Finance Operations Team Lead @ WorkMotion


That means engaging the right person at the right time, using what you know about each customer from past interactions. It’s an approach we call[Financial Relationship Management](https://upflow.io/financial-relationship-management) .


Here’s a typical escalation timeline. Adjust the timing to your payment terms and customer segments:


When What to send Tone


A few days before the due date Friendly reminder email Helpful


On the due date Reminder email with a payment link Polite


1 to 14 days overdue Follow-up emails Polite, assuming it's an oversight


15 to 30 days overdue Firmer email and a phone call Direct


Around 30 days overdue Collection letter sample 1: formal reminder Formal


Around 45 days overdue Collection letter sample 2: service restriction warning Firm


Around 60 days overdue Collection letter sample 3: final notice before legal action Urgent


90+ days overdue Collection letter sample 4: legal notice Legal


The early emails should assume the delay is unintentional, since most late payments come down to a missed email or an internal approval. As the invoice ages, each message should get more direct. By the third outreach, a phone call often resolves things faster than another email, and it shows you’re serious while still valuing the relationship.


If emails and calls don’t work, move to collection letters. Save the legal notice for when every reasonable attempt to collect has failed.


## How to Prevent Late Payments Before You Need a Collection Letter


The best way to avoid sending collection letters is to make on-time payment the easy option from the start. That comes down to clear terms, timely reminders, easy ways to pay and knowing which customers need closer attention.


1. **Set clear payment terms.** Agree on due dates, accepted payment methods and penalties for late payment in the contract, so both sides know what to expect.
2. **Send reminders before invoices are due.** A friendly reminder a few days before the due date often prevents the delay altogether.
3. **Offer flexible payment options.** Accept cards, bank transfers and[ACH](https://upflow.io/blog/business-to-business-payments/ach-credit-vs-ach-debit) payments, so customers can pay the way that suits them.
4. **Incentivize early payment.** Small[discounts for early payment](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/net-30-terms#early-payment-discounts-210-net-30-and-more) give customers a reason to pay before the due date.
5. **Segment your customers.** Group customers by payment history, so you can automate reminders for most and give personal attention to the ones who need a call.
6. **Automate the routine work.** Connecting your collections process to your billing, accounting,[ERP and CRM](https://upflow.io/blog/accounting-software/erp-vs-crm) systems keeps invoice data up to date without manual spreadsheet work.
